title: Single-Pass Linear Scan for Longest Consecutive Zeros
approach_explanation: The problem asks for the maximum length of consecutive zeros in a binary array. We can solve this efficiently by iterating through the array. Whenever we encounter a zero, we start counting the length of the contiguous block of zeros using a nested while loop. We track the maximum length encountered across all such blocks. Once a block of zeros ends (i.e., we hit a 1 or the end of the array), we compare its length with our running maximum and update it. This allows us to find the correct answer in a single forward pass per test case.

code_breakdown.section_title: Test Case Initialization and Array Reading
code_breakdown.explanation: Read the number of test cases `t`. For each test case, read the array size `n` and populate the vector `v` with `n` binary integers.
Initialize `max_op = 0` to store the maximum consecutive zeros found. Iterate through the array using index `i`.

code_breakdown.section_title: Counting Contiguous Zeros and Updating Maximum
code_breakdown.explanation: When `v[i] == 0`, start a nested loop to count the number of consecutive zeros (`ops`) while `i < n` and `v[i] == 0`. Increment `i` accordingly. Update `max_op` with the maximum of its current value and `ops`.
Print the maximum length of blank spaces found for the current testcase, followed by a newline.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: For each testcase, the outer loop runs at most $n$ times, and the inner while loop only increments the loop variable `i` when it encounters `0`. Each element of the array is visited at most twice across both loops. Thus, the time complexity per testcase is linear with respect to the array size $n$. Over $t$ testcases, total time complexity is $O(\sum n)$, which is well within the 1-second limit for $\sum n \le 10^5$.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: A `std::vector<int>` of size $n$ is allocated for each testcase to store the elements. Hence, the auxiliary space complexity is $O(n)$ per test case.

strengths: Clean and simple implementation that is easy to understand.
best_practices_feedback: Use `std::ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(NULL);` to speed up competitive programming I/O operations.
Avoid `#include<bits/stdc++.h>` in production codebases, though acceptable in competitive programming.
Consider declaring variables closer to their usage rather than at the top of scopes.

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Instead of storing the array elements in a `std::vector`, we can read each integer on the fly in a single loop, maintaining the current count of consecutive zeros and the maximum count. This reduces space complexity from $O(n)$ to $O(1)$.
